text: In 2012, Felix Baumgartner stepped off a balloon almost thirty-nine kilometres up.
Near forty kilometres, a cubic metre of air has a mass of under four grams. That's about three hundred times thinner than at sea level.
So the fall kept speeding up, and thirty-four seconds in, he passed the speed of sound.
Fifty seconds in came his top speed: one thousand, three hundred and fifty-seven point six kilometres an hour.
That's Mach one point two five, in a fall that lasted four minutes and twenty seconds in all.
Look at the gap. He passed the speed of sound at thirty-four seconds, and kept speeding up for sixteen seconds more.
Then, at fifty seconds, the speed stopped growing, with the ground still a long way below.
It wasn't the sound barrier. He had passed that sixteen seconds earlier. Something else was pushing back.
So what pushed back? The full video on our channel has the answer. Like and subscribe so you don't miss the next one.
